Numerical polology: towards next-generation model-building for cosmology
Will Barker, Will Handley, Michael Hobson, Anthony Lasenby, Carlo Marzo, Alessandro Santoni, Leonardo Torcellini

Abstract
The dark sector need not be restricted to simple field content. Indeed, simple bosonic configurations, such as scalar-tensor or dark photon models, contrast with the much richer picture painted by many ultraviolet scenarios. Polology is the study of propagator poles, which correspond to particle states in any given theory. We outline a numerical polology framework for discovering perturbative, ghost-free models with consistent interactions, which produces theoretical model priors by sampling the coupling space. The method is tested on tensor field theories of up to rank three. Subsequent observational constraint pipelines are illustrated for black hole superradiance (M33 X-7), dynamical dark energy (DESI DR2, Pantheon and SH0ES) and gravitational waves (GWTC-3).



I  Introduction

Theories are data models

Particle dark matter, along with many ultraviolet scenarios, suggest that additional low-energy degrees of freedom remain to be discovered. In a popular scenario, bosonic fields on flat spacetime will form a (generally non-renormalizable) effective field theory (EFT) with action

\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})=\int\mathrm{d}^{4}x\,\sum_{i}\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}\,\mathcal{O}^{i},

(1)

in which operators with mass dimension
[\mathcal{O}^{i}]=n
are parameterised by couplings
\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}\sim\Lambda^{4-n}
, where
\Lambda
is a cutoff.

From the theoretician’s perspective,
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
is a
functional
of the field content; yet it may also be viewed as a
function
of the couplings
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
, and it is this latter dependence which we choose to emphasise. Theories of physics are inherently subordinate to the observed phenomena: any action
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
is ultimately a data model, for which the couplings
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
are model parameters. Given observational data
D
, the relative worth of a theory is then determined by the evidence

\mathcal{Z}(D)=\int\mathrm{d}\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}\,\mathcal{L}(D|\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})\,\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}),

(2)

where
\mathcal{L}(D|\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
is the likelihood of
D
in the context of
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
, and
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
is the prior probability of the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
. In precision cosmology, great advances have been made in collecting
D
and efficiently computing
\mathcal{L}(D|\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
for the available
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
that seem best-motivated; such fits are systematised in global-fitting frameworks such as
GAMBIT

[
12
,
13
,
107
]
, which evaluate
\mathcal{L}(D|\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
— and, in a Bayesian analysis, the evidence
Eq.

2
itself — for a given
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
. The complementary theoretical programme for producing candidate
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
is also very active; in relative terms, though, it is less systematic (note counterexamples such as
[
10
,
33
]
,
[
34
,
113
]
and
[
36
,
54
,
50
]
), while the need for efficient computation of
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
is often overlooked.

The ability to compute
\mathcal{L}(D|\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
for some
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
is called
predictivity
. Regardless of renormalizability, a theory of the form given in
Eq.

1
is endowed with predictivity by the systematics of quantum field theory, and by nothing else
[
111
,
35
,
28
,
25
]
. Quantum field theory also imposes strict constraints on the permissible values of the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
, and it is helpful to interpret these constraints as contributing to
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
. For example, the
\mathcal{O}^{i}
which are quadratic in the fields determine the particle spectrum: the unitarity of the
S
-matrix typically excludes portions of the corresponding
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space. For the free spectrum, this is the requirement of positive propagator residues (no ghosts) and real pole masses (no tachyons); it is distinct from, though complementary to, the energy-dependent perturbative-unitarity bounds that such global fits impose on the interacting couplings
[
31
,
32
]
.

Nor is this ‘quantum’ contribution to
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
ever
too
restrictive: it avoids contrived models whose
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
are subject to ad hoc tunings, i.e., conditionings of the prior which cannot be justified without knowledge of the ultraviolet physics. Specifically, it is the symmetries of the quadratic sector which dictate all the non-linear operators according to the perturbative Noether procedure
[
19
,
48
]
. It is thus not permitted to shrink
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
via any tunings of the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
which eliminate symmetric interactions; doing so would jeopardise the radiative stability of the model
[
78
,
79
]
. Rather, the
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
for a symmetric model may actually be
expanded
into the space of non-symmetric theories, but this process is also tightly controlled. The organising principle is that small, symmetry-breaking
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
inherit some radiative protection, and are technically natural
[
116
]
. Valid
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
must be derived from all these quantum considerations, and many others besides.

Scalable model-building

The class of theories in
Eq.

1
successfully describes all the fundamental bosons that are currently known to exist, and thus offers a conservative infrared foundation for new physics. The coordinate invariance of linearised gravity — as a symmetry — gives rise uniquely to non-linear general relativity
[
40
]
(see also
[
26
]
) and its predictive EFT extension
[
41
,
42
]
; the Maxwell theory meanwhile gives rise to Yang–Mills. Small symmetry-breaking masses for both the vector gauge boson and graviton are technically natural; the former are actually observed in the weak sector, where the symmetry is restored by the Higgs mechanism.

Many proposals for new physics in cosmology concern spin-zero species, but there is also a literature on spin-one
[
84
,
53
,
29
,
90
,
91
,
18
,
30
]
, spin-two
[
22
,
23
]
and higher-spin
[
6
,
43
,
64
]
particles. For these spins respectively, the Klein–Gordon
[
68
,
51
]
, Proca
[
96
]
, Fierz–Pauli
[
47
,
46
]
and Singh–Hagen
[
102
]
actions are normally used as a foundation, from which interactions are attempted to be derived.
1
1

1

Of course, interactions from Klein–Gordon and Singh–Hagen theories are respectively nil and problematic, see e.g.
[
39
,
69
,
115
]
.
For comprehensive model comparison, however, it is important to understand the full range of possibilities, and in particular we observe that:

“
Not all theories can be described just by specifying the particle spin; the field content of the action leads to its own phenomenological implications.
”

For example, a symmetric, rank-two tensor field can propagate a spin-two particle, but it can also propagate a scalar if Klein–Gordon theory is written in terms of the trace. This does not affect the phenomenology, but when
multiple
fields are used, the number of possible interaction operators and constraining symmetries grows rapidly. Interactions (i.e. non-linearities) are absolutely crucial to phenomenological signatures. The fact that the quantum
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
may be hard to compute in such cases does not automatically exclude them from participating in the dark sector as technically natural EFTs, and we are in principle obliged to consider them.

The proliferation of the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
due to extended field content may seem undesirable, since extra parameters are sometimes assumed to weaken predictivity through an associated Occam penalty
[
59
]
. In practice, however, this question may only be decided by a detailed application of
Eq.

2
, whose intimate dependence on
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
just reinforces the importance of correctly computing the prior. Moreover, within the bounds set by
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
, it is not unreasonable to expect that high
\mathcal{L}(D|\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
and competitive
\mathcal{Z}(D)
may
only
be achievable in the context of some richly parametric
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
, whose specific interactions can be used to explain some equally specific signal in
D
.

In any case, the volume and quality of
D
will continue to grow with each generation of surveys. It is thus important that our capacity for the systematic manufacture of
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
scales appropriately, and this calls for a high degree of automation.

In this work

A framework is developed for efficiently computing the unitary prior
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
on the couplings
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
which parameterise the free sector of
Eq.

1
— i.e., the operators
\mathcal{O}^{i}
which are quadratic in the fields. A numerical approach is also available for quantum corrections: these are necessary for constraining interaction couplings under the same framework, which will be the subject of the companion paper. Even at tree level, however, there is scope for connecting
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
to cosmological observables: some basic observational constraints on a new Stueckelberg extension of massive gravity are illustrated.

Our technique —
numerical polology
— fully embraces the interpretation of
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
as a data model, by promoting
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space to the central object of study.

This kind of approach has yet to be established in cosmology, but it has a clear precedent in particle physics through the
SARAH

[
7
]
,
SOFTSUSY

[
105
,
106
]
and
SPheno

[
94
,
93
]
infrastructures. There are, however, important differences in our approach. Firstly, the method admits non-renormalisable theories, with arbitrarily many higher-rank fields. Secondly, the sampling procedure is incorporated into the algorithm, which allows extensions beyond
model testing
and into
model discovery
.

The remainder of this paper is organised as follows.
Section

II
provides illustrative examples of the method.
Section

III
develops the theory underlying the algorithm, and provides details of the computational implementation. Conclusions follow in
Section

IV
, and there are several technical appendices. We use natural units
\hbar\equiv c\equiv 1
throughout, and the particle physics signature
(+,-,-,-)
.

II  Examples

Numerical polology

The particle spectrum of a theory is determined by the poles of the propagator, the study of which is called
polology

[
112
]
.

The formal polology algorithm for computing the free particle spectrum and associated unitarity of
Eq.

1
has been known since the work of Van Nieuwenhuizen and Sezgin
[
110
,
85
,
86
,
101
,
100
,
70
,
66
,
67
,
81
,
92
,
77
,
78
,
82
,
83
]
, but the technique is computationally expensive. Computer algebra implementations such as
PSALTer

[
17
,
16
]
,
Kummitus

[
80
]
and others
[
71
,
72
,
73
,
74
]
have recently been developed, but these scale poorly with the complexity of the theory due to expression swell. For a scalable approach, the only avenue is numerical.

In this section the scope of the method is illustrated with a series of examples.
Section

II.1
considers simple models, before the approach is used as a tool for theoretical discovery in
Section

II.2
.
Section

II.3
extends beyond theory to show that the framework natively accommodates data-driven constraints, and interactions are introduced in
Section

II.4
.

II.1
Tuned theories

The unitary region defines a prior
\pi(\Theta)
on the compactified coupling space. The compactification in
Eq.

5
places an implicit standard Cauchy measure on each coupling,
\mathrm{d}\mu\propto\prod_{i}\mathrm{d}\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}/(1+\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}^{2})
— heavy-tailed, symmetric under
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}\leftrightarrow 1/\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
, and uniform in
\Theta
. The virtue of the hypercube is that this uniform measure is a product, so its projection onto any subset of the
\Theta
remains uniform; structure in the marginal panels of
\pi(\Theta)
therefore tracks the unitarity boundary itself, rather than any coordinate Jacobian. This follows the standard nested-sampling convention
[
45
]
, already central to the early particle physics global fits of Feroz, Hobson and collaborators
[
44
]
, and is forfeited by the hyperspherical chart adopted for high-rank theories below (see
Fig.

6
).

Such a prior is informed only by the requirements of quantum field theory, and thus forms an absolute basis for subsequent phenomenological constraints. The availability of
Eq.

6
means that
\pi(\Theta)
is known analytically, but this will not always be the case when scaling to more complicated models. With this scaling in mind, the distribution
\pi(\Theta)
is best encoded numerically by the density of some finite population of samples. These are generated by a sampling algorithm, driven by a loss function which is designed to reward the generation of unitary samples. Depending on the application, the loss function may also select for desirable features in the spectrum, such as particles of specific spin or parity.

In the present case, the samples are uniformly distributed within the unitary region, with contours at
0.68
and
0.95
confidence levels determined by boundary-corrected kernel density estimation (KDE), as implemented in
anesthetic

[
57
]
. These contours are illustrative: the small number of
\sim 10^{4}
samples results in visibly ragged edges, but the square shape of the unitary region is still clear.

Stueckelberg gravity

Whilst
Eqs.

3
and
7
are well known models, it is also possible to study new theories. The most general Stueckelberg extension of massive gravity in which transverse diffeomorphism invariance is restored is
2
2

2

II.2
Untuned theories

Tuning hierarchies

Actually, the theories in
Eqs.

3
,
7
and
9
already have part of the ‘quantum’ prior baked in. This is evident, because in all cases the dimension
N
of the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space is smaller than the number of operators (i.e. the number of terms corresponding to independent index contractions) in
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
, and this can be viewed as a result of tuning some more general
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
to agree with various quantum requirements. A consequence of this tuning is visible in
Figs.

1
,
2
and
3
, where the unitary regions are seen to occupy a finite
volume
of the remaining
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space.

The
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space of untuned models is not generally expected to contain unitary volumes, but will instead be punctuated by unitary
hypersurfaces
of lower dimension
d<N
. These hypersurfaces correspond to tuned theories.

It is possible to tune for a unitary mass spectrum directly, or to tune for the emergence of new gauge symmetries which happen to admit unitary mass spectra. The two methods are not equivalent, but both can be valid so long as care is taken in the interpretation of the results and – crucially – the way in which any
\mathcal{L}(D|\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
are computed
[
111
,
35
,
28
,
25
]
. Symmetry tuning offers stability against radiative corrections, and pushes the cutoff parametrically beyond any native scales when interactions are included. Unitarity tuning typically results in a low cutoff, but the resulting models may still be technically natural EFTs. Tunings can and do occur recursively within sufficiently complex theories. The hierarchy of features that may be identified in this way is illustrated in
Fig.

4
. It will next be shown that numerical polology is well-suited to finding such features.

Figure 4:
More complicated models require the hierarchical identification of unitary theories, which lie on tuned surfaces in
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space. In surfaces defined by unitarity alone, rather than by the emergence of protective gauge symmetries, the validity of the theory may be limited by radiative corrections.

Figure 5:
The
N=3
parameter space of
Eq.

11
and its unitary structure.
Left:
as an example of
Fig.

4
, a schematic of the compactified hypercube, with the two unitarity-tuned hypersurfaces and the corresponding healthy quadrants highlighted in blue.
Centre:
the unitary
\pi(\Theta)
of
Eq.

11
.
Right:
classification of
\pi(\Theta)
into Proca (green) and Klein–Gordon-like (red) branches, with the numerical trajectories associated with the emergence of gauge symmetries shown in black. Starting points
A
and
B
are chosen from the Klein–Gordon-like branch;
C
and
D
from the Proca branch. Meanwhile, spin-zero symmetries emerge from
A
and
C
, while spin-one symmetries emerge from
B
and
D
. Of these,
B
and
C
indicate technical naturalness.

Both branches are a product of unitarity tuning, and may be classified according to the spins of the massive poles. Neither branch is protected by any gauge symmetry, and so they may also be classified according to technical naturalness. This is done by numerically computing the trajectories in
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space which lead to the emergence of gauge symmetries — the details are provided in
Section

III
. Points from either branch have two such trajectories, corresponding to the spin sectors (zero or one) in which the symmetries arise. One trajectory tunnels to the opposing branch through the low-
\pi(\Theta)
void, while the other adheres to the high-
\pi(\Theta)
surface of the same branch. The latter trajectories correspond to the technically natural deformations of each theory. All trajectories terminate in the massless limit
\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{3}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{3}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{3}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{3}}}}=0
. In the Proca branch, the emergent symmetry is that of Maxwell theory; the other branch recovers a (transverse) symmetry of the spin-one sector.

Effective model-dimension

Under the interpretation of theories as data models, as set out in
Section

I
, it is important to understand the effective number of model parameters. In the tuned case, the unitary subvolume simply inherits the dimensionality
d=N
of the parent
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space. For untuned theories,
d
is a derived parameter.

All the branches derived from all the parent actions in
Section

II.2
correspond to free theories of a single massive particle, and so it may be expected that the effective
d=1
— the particle mass — in all cases: this is certainly true when phenomenological constraints are applied to the free theory alone, as will be seen in
Section

II.3
. It is shown in
Sections

II.4
and
F
, however, that quantum corrections from the interacting theory
also
depend on the free couplings, and that they do so in combinations other than the particle mass formulae.

It thus seems safest to track the full geometric
d
, and it is discussed in
Appendices

G
and
C
how this can be estimated numerically from the chain of samples that encodes the prior. In
Table

1
, the effective
d
for the discovered branches of the various untuned theories are shown.

II.3
Astroparticle physics

Tree-level phenomenology

The derived quantities associated with numerical polology admit various phenomenological constraints, which can be applied as multiplicative weights to the ‘quantum’ prior, thereby producing a tighter composite prior.

This is demonstrated using three independent probes, applied to the theory in
Eq.

9
. For all probes, derived masses are exploited. This requires us to fix the reference scale
\mu
in
Eq.

5
, i.e. the unit in which the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
of non-zero mass dimension is measured — the computation of mass dimensions is discussed in
Section

III
. Phenomenologically, attention is drawn to mass scales which maximally affect the observables; in astrophysics and cosmology these are very low, at
m\ll$1\text{\,}\mathrm{eV}$
. An appropriate choice of
\mu
is close to this scale, and thus shields the numerics from its small value.
5
5

5

In principle, numerical problems could still arise for untuned theories, for which the priors are obtained by sweeping sick and unwanted poles into a hierarchy — see
Appendix

G
. Increasing this hierarchy is numerically costly, requiring higher-precision arithmetic without which the pathological sector may appear at a phenomenologically relevant scale if
\mu\ll$1\text{\,}\mathrm{eV}$
. To overcome this problem, it suffices to simply neglect the sick poles in phenomenological computations.

The most rigorous cosmological pipelines tend to assume general relativity as the underlying gravitational framework, into which ‘modules’ of new physics are injected. Consequently, the model in
Eq.

9
offers an awkward case-study: as a theory of massive gravity, different from general relativity, its eventual non-linear completion may call for arduous pipeline revisions.

Since the following constraints are intended to be illustrative, we will mostly gloss over this limitation (see
Appendices

D
and
E
for full details). Indeed, due to these and other difficulties, ‘modified’ theories of gravity are not presently the most promising frontier for new physics, whilst the dark matter problem presents as a more useful target.

Superradiance

Ultralight bosons trigger superradiant instabilities of spinning black holes (BHs), so BH observations exclude boson masses within a corresponding window
[
11
]
. In its basic form, superradiance is sensitive only to the Lagrangian itself, and is agnostic with respect to the dynamical configuration of the fields. Constraints arise for any BH whose horizon is comparable to the Compton wavelength of the boson. Heavy species are constrained by X-ray binaries (XRBs) and gravitational wave (GW) events; light species by active galactic nuclei. The BH spin, and thus the quality of the constraint, depends strongly on the population from which the BH is drawn.

Beyond the free mass, superradiant instability is additionally sensitive to the boson spin, and to self-interactions. A thorough superradiance pipeline will thus be able to take advantage of the full tower of derived parameters in numerical polology. This becomes useful if, for example, an improved understanding of BH demography reveals gaps that cannot be explained by astrophysical processes alone. The prior in
Fig.

3
is reweighted under the following hypothesis:

“
The massive spin-zero particle predicted by
Eq.

9
is susceptible to superradiant instabilities near BHs.
”

This is done using observations of M33 X-7
[
89
]
, a stellar-mass XRB probing
m\sim${10}^{-13}\text{\,}\mathrm{eV}{10}^{-11}\text{\,}\mathrm{eV}$
. The weight is computed using the
BHSR
software of Hoof
et al.

[
61
]
, with further details given in
Appendix

D
. As shown in
Fig.

7
(left), superradiance excludes
63.8\%
of the prior volume at
\mu=$1.43\text{\times}{10}^{-12}\text{\,}\mathrm{eV}$
.

Dark energy

In the canonical quintessence scenario, a massive scalar field has an effective equation of state that transitions from
w\approx-1
to
w\approx 0
at the epoch
m\sim H(z)

[
108
,
76
]
. Variations on this theme are known to strongly affect the Hubble tension via early dark energy models
[
95
,
65
]
, and may be useful in response to recent signals for dynamical dark energy at late times
[
4
,
2
]
. Such effects can, in principle, be constrained to as far back as big bang nucleosynthesis, beyond which the expansion history becomes speculative. The prior in
Fig.

3
is reweighted under the following hypothesis:

“
The massive spin-zero particle predicted by
Eq.

9
is responsible for 100% of dark energy.
”

This is done using the DESI DR2 BAO measurements
[
2
]
combined with Pantheon and SH0ES supernovae
[
99
]
. Our pipeline follows the analysis of Ormondroyd
et al.

[
87
,
88
]
, with further details given in
Appendix

E
. The resulting constraint on the spin-zero mass, shown in
Fig.

7
(middle), excludes
90.7\%
of the prior volume at
\mu=$1.41\text{\times}{10}^{-32}\text{\,}\mathrm{eV}$
.

Graviton dispersion

A massive graviton modifies the dispersion relation of GWs, causing frequency-dependent propagation speeds that are detectable in compact binary coalescence signals. The prior in
Fig.

3
is reweighted under the following hypothesis:

“
The massive spin-two particle predicted by
Eq.

9
is identified as the graviton which mediates GWs.
”

The GWTC-3 combined analysis of 43 binary BH events yields the bound
m\leq$2.42\text{\times}{10}^{-23}\text{\,}\mathrm{eV}$
at
90\%
credibility
[
1
]
. As shown in
Fig.

7
(right), the GWTC-3 bound excludes
20.1\%
of the prior volume at
\mu=$1.52\text{\times}{10}^{-22}\text{\,}\mathrm{eV}$
.

In summary, the example of
Eq.

9
— despite being a somewhat arbitrary theory — demonstrates that the method is well suited to the imposition of observational constraints. We do not extend here to actual model selection.

II.4
Interactions

Interactions

Many more observational constraints become accessible when interactions are included, so it is essential that the proposed framework accommodates these. As mentioned in
Section

I
, the ‘quantum’ prior on the interaction couplings must meet various strict requirements.

Whilst the interacting sector is not the main focus of this work, it is helpful to provide an example through the Fierz–Pauli theory in
Eq.

3
. The field can be canonically normalized with
M_{\text{Pl}}
, so that

is replaced by

Detuning

Eq.

20
illustrates how the introduction of the Fierz–Pauli mass through
\mathchoice{\bar{\theta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{2}}}}{\bar{\theta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{2}}}}{\bar{\theta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{2}}}}{\bar{\theta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{2}}}}
detunes — not only the Fierz–Pauli mass term itself — but also the kinetic structure in the linearization of the Einstein–Hilbert term.

As mentioned in
Section

II.2
, the tuning of the free theory is critical to the health of the model. In this case, however, the effects vanish along with the graviton mass as
\mathchoice{\bar{\theta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{2}}}}{\bar{\theta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{2}}}}{\bar{\theta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{2}}}}{\bar{\theta}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[3.98613pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.45pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.75pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{2}}}}\to 0
, coinciding with the emergence of the gauge symmetry, and this is an indicator of technical naturalness.

Formulae such as those given in
Eq.

20
may be readily obtained for more general models. In
Appendix

F
the corresponding radiative corrections are shown with all possible cubic and quartic algebraic couplings included. Based on such expressions, it is apparent that numerical sampling procedures may be used to reconstruct consistent interactions — either with strict closure under renormalization, or with technically natural limits — on top of the tree-level analyses in
Sections

II.1
,
II.2
and
II.3
.

We now proceed in
Section

III
to discuss the technical details of the approach, with an emphasis on the tree-level theory.

III  Theoretical development

Mass spectra

In this section, we will outline how the priors in
Figs.

1
,
2
,
3
and
5
may be obtained.
Figs.

6
and
1
require a separate implementation, whose discussion is deferred to
Appendix

As explained in
[
17
,
16
]
, the technical details of the polology algorithm, as applied to models of the form given in
Eq.

1
, differ between the massive and massless sectors due to the change in the little group. In the massive case, it suffices to work in the representation of spin
J
and parity
P
; in the massless case, a full component decomposition of the fields is required.

Fortunately, our focus on phenomenologically relevant models allows us to avoid the massless sector in our analysis, since additional radiative degrees of freedom are excluded by the thermal history.
6
6

6

More thoroughly, this is only true for populated species in thermal equilibrium
[
55
,
20
]
.
At every numerically sampled
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
, we thus work with the full suite of massive poles, and seek to navigate the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space on the basis of their physical health. Beyond this restriction, we will also limit our analysis to parity-preserving theories.
7
7

7

The algorithm for parity-violating theories has been worked out in
[
16
]
, based on work by Karananas in
[
66
]
, and may be applied in future work.

Once the

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)

\displaystyle=\sum_{n}\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)k^{n},

(22)

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta;k)

\displaystyle=\sum_{n}\mathchoice{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)k^{n},

which gives rise to a block singular value decomposition problem, as follows. Truncating the ansatz
\mathchoice{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
at degree
N_{J^{P}}\,(\dim\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)-1)
, where
N_{J^{P}}
is the highest non-vanishing order in
\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)
, yields a finite linear system
\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)\cdot\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}=0
, where
\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}
stacks the
\mathchoice{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
, and where the block matrix
\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)
is built from the
\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)
in a Toeplitz pattern

\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)\equiv\begin{pmatrix}\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(0)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(0)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(0)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(0)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)&\cdots&0\\
\vdots&&\vdots\\
\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(N_{J^{P}})}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(N_{J^{P}})}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(N_{J^{P}})}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(N_{J^{P}})}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)&\ddots&0\\
0&&\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(0)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(0)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(0)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(0)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)\\
\vdots&&\vdots\\
0&\cdots&\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(N_{J^{P}})}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(N_{J^{P}})}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(N_{J^{P}})}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(N_{J^{P}})}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)\end{pmatrix}.

(23)

The genuine
\mathchoice{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta;k)
may then be reassembled from the solution for
\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}
.

Masses and tachyons

Once the symmetries have been found, the regularised wave operator

\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)\equiv\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)+\sum_{a}\mathchoice{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta;k)\cdot\mathchoice{\mathsf{v}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta;k),

(24)

may be inverted, and this inverse is proportional to the propagator. The poles of the propagator correspond to the physical states, and must also correspond to the roots of
\det\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)
.

Numerically, a candidate spectrum of poles can be found without symbolic manipulation via a polynomial eigenvalue problem in
k
— though
Appendix

G
presents an alternative approach based on the Vandermonde and Frobenius methods. Because the construction in
Eq.

22
does not give rise to normalised
\mathchoice{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta;k)
, this spectrum will generally be polluted by spurious ‘gauge’ poles, though these are readily stripped by comparing their null eigenvectors with the gauge sector of the kernel. The physical poles are associated with null eigenvectors, denoted by

\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta))\cdot\mathchoice{\mathsf{u}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{u}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{u}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{u}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)=0.

(25)

The poles occur in pairs, because
\det\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{\text{reg}}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)
is formally known to be a polynomial in
k^{2}
; for each zero of this polynomial, the principal second root is identified with the mass
\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
of the corresponding pair of poles. This naturally extends the convention of positive masses for real poles to the complex case, which now have positive real part. In general, only real poles are healthy, since

\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)^{2}>0,

(26)

is the no-tachyon criterion.

Residues and ghosts

The no-ghost criterion depends on the pole residue

\mathchoice{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)>0,

(27)

which was shown in
[
17
]
to be given by

\mathchoice{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)\equiv\mathop{\mathrm{Res}}_{k^{2}\to\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)^{2}}\left(P\,{\rm tr}\,\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{+}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{+}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{+}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{+}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)\right),

(28)

where
\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{+}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{+}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{+}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{+}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)
is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of
\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)
. Even with sampled
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
, obtaining the pseudoinverse remains a symbolic problem. A numerical alternative follows from the matrix
\mathchoice{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)
whose columns are the
\mathchoice{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{v}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta;\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta))
, and which defines the non-gauge projection

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathsf{w}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{w}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{w}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{w}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)

\displaystyle\equiv\left[\mathsf{1}-\mathchoice{\mathsf{P}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{P}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{P}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{P}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)\right]\cdot\mathchoice{\mathsf{u}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{u}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{u}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{u}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta),

(29)

\displaystyle\mathchoice{\mathsf{P}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{P}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{P}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{P}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)

\displaystyle\equiv\mathchoice{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)\cdot\left(\mathchoice{\mathsf{V}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)\cdot\mathchoice{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)\right)^{-1}\cdot\mathchoice{\mathsf{V}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{V}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta),

of the massive null eigenvectors. For real, positive
\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
, the residue in
Eq.

28
is then given by the expansion

\displaystyle\mathchoice{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)=2P\Bigg[

\displaystyle\sum_{n}n\,\left|\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)\right|^{n-2}

(30)

\displaystyle\times\mathchoice{\mathsf{w}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{w}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{w}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{w}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)\cdot\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)\cdot\mathchoice{\mathsf{w}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{w}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{w}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\mathsf{w}_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)\Bigg]^{-1},

where the modulus is introduced to provide a simple analytic continuation to complex poles, though the interpretation as the residue is lost in this case. Since
\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)
is Hermitian for all
n
, so
\mathchoice{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
is always real by construction.

Mass dimensions

So far, the mass dimensions of the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
have not been specified. Indeed, the fields themselves only acquire a definite canonical dimension once the spectrum has been computed, and the same must be true of the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
. Let
\mathchoice{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}\equiv[\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}]
, whilst
[\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)]\equiv 1
. By this point in the calculation, the
\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
are numerically available, and a rescaling of the mass unit
\mu\to\beta\mu
so that
\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}\to\beta^{\mathchoice{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.66785pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[0.86128pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}}\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}
, and
\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)\to\beta\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
, yields

\sum_{i}\mathchoice{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}\,\frac{\partial\ln\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)}{\partial\ln\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}}=1.

(31)

Any choice of
\mathchoice{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}
that satisfies
Eq.

31
for all
\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
is valid. To ensure that the Lagrangian density has the correct mass dimension, under the usual convention that propagating bosons have a canonical dimension of unity, integer solutions are sought with
\min_{i}\mathchoice{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{d^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}=0
.

It is this control over the mass dimensions that allows us to impose the phenomenological reference scale
\mu
used in
Section

II.3
.

Technical naturalness

Returning to the question of gauge symmetries, the singular values
\mathchoice{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
of
\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)
as defined in
Eq.

23
provide a useful diagnostic for the proximity of the theory to a gauge-symmetric configuration. To navigate towards such a surface from a given sample
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
, we perform steepest descent on a chosen
\mathchoice{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
. The gradient is provided by the singular-value analogue of the Hellmann–Feynman theorem

\frac{\partial\mathchoice{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\sigma_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)}{\partial\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}}=\Re\left[\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{u}}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{u}}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{u}}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{u}}^{{{\dagger}}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}\cdot\frac{\partial\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)}{\partial\mathchoice{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{\theta^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}}\cdot\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}\right],

(32)

where
\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{u}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{u}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{u}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{u}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}
and
\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{v}}_{{{a_{{J^{P}}}}}}}
are the corresponding left and right singular vectors of
\mathchoice{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\bar{\mathsf{O}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)
. Because each
\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)
is linear in the couplings, the derivatives may be precomputed.

Sampling likelihood

So far, it was only described how to numerically obtain physical quantities from a given sample
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
. It is now necessary to efficiently generate samples of the prior distribution
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
. For performant sampling of high-
N

\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space, it is appropriate to use a nested sampler
[
103
,
104
]
(see implementations in
[
45
,
56
,
27
,
114
]
). An additional advantage of nested sampling is its natural integration with the Bayesian framework set out in
Eq.

2
. In this context, the loss function mentioned in
Section

II.1
itself corresponds to a likelihood.

There are many ways to construct a heuristic likelihood for quantum field theory.
8
8

8

The posterior of one experiment is the prior of the next. In this framework, model-building begins with the empirically established laws of quantum field theory, which give rise to
\mathcal{L}(\text{QFT}|\theta)
. Subsequent experiments give rise to the
\mathcal{L}(D|\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
of
Eq.

2
. Note that a
uniform
prior is assumed when working with
\mathcal{L}(\text{QFT}|\theta)
, and the usual ambiguity remains in finding appropriate coordinates for
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space.
Focussing on the tuned theories of
Section

II.1
, for which the spectra are already known, the goal is to find the sub-volume of the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space which is unitary. Since unitarity is boolean — either present or not — it is necessary to define a ‘fuzzy’ continuation by means of which the sampler is driven by a unitarity-violation penalty; this can be done with the choice

\log\mathcal{L}(\text{QFT}|\theta)=\sum_{J,P}\sum_{s_{J^{P}}}\Bigl[\mathcal{U}\!\left(\mathchoice{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)\right)\\
+\mathcal{U}\!\left(-\left|\Im\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)\right|\right)\Bigr].

(33)

Eq.

33
is a sum over contributions from all the poles, in which the function
\mathcal{U}
acts on
\mathchoice{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
and
m(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
, since they share the same mass dimension. According to
Eqs.

26
and
27
, the central requirement of
\mathcal{U}
is sensitivity to the sign of its argument. Work done by the nested sampler in the healthy region is always wasted, and so we adopt
\mathcal{U}(x)=0
for
x>0
. By the same logic, such plateaus should be
avoided
in the sick region.

The transition between sick and healthy regions is not always via the origin:
\mathchoice{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{Z_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
and
\mathchoice{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}{m_{{{s_{{J^{P}}}}}}}(\theta)
vary according to a (potentially very complicated) problem in algebraic geometry, which means that changes of sign may also occur across singularities in
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space. Consequently, infinite unitarity violation must be mapped smoothly back to zero; this can be achieved with

\mathcal{U}(x)\equiv\begin{cases}0,&x>0,\\
-\dfrac{2\,|x|^{u}}{1+|x|^{2u}},&x\leq 0,\end{cases}

(34)

where
u
is a global parameter which can assist convergence in cases where the power-law near a sign change is extreme — we adopt
u=0.5
in this work.

The construction in
Eq.

33
ensures that the likelihood is maximised at
\mathcal{L}(\text{QFT}|\theta)=1
by unitarity. Nested sampling does not maximise the likelihood, but instead reflects the distribution of its volume. It is thus necessary to filter out the
\mathcal{L}(\text{QFT}|\theta)<1
samples in the final chain. This is the procedure that leads to the prior distributions of tuned theories shown in
Figs.

1
,
2
and
3
, and it is also effective for the simple untuned theory shown in
Fig.

5
.

For more complex untuned theories, the case is altered (see
Appendix

G
for an example implementation): the final samples must land on set-of-measure-zero hypersurfaces, and so root-finding becomes central to a successful algorithm. It is imagined that the application to untuned theories will be far more useful than in the tuned case, since this allows hitherto unknown theories to be discovered.

IV  Conclusions

Overview

The literature contains a large and growing plethora of new physics models. By mutual exclusion, most (perhaps all) of these theories cannot be realised in nature, and the theoretical return on investment seems especially low given the historical rate at which the standard models of particle physics and cosmology have actually been updated. More precisely, the problem is not that there are
too many
models, but rather that the techniques for constructing them have not been adequately mechanised.

This work proposes a framework for systematically exploring theory-space, using
numerical polology
. The method is restricted to perturbative bosonic degrees of freedom. Within these bounds, the need for theoretical innovation is minimised, since quantum field theory already provides the complete set of principles (no more, no less) needed for the development of predictive theories. Sampling is central to the method, allowing it to integrate naturally with the techniques of model selection in precision cosmology. In particular, the unitary
\pi(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
is a principled, field-theoretic prior over the free couplings. Bayesian global fits already place explicit priors on such couplings
[
13
,
3
]
, but typically as generic (flat or logarithmic) ranges supplemented by theory-validity cuts — perturbativity, EFT-validity and partial-wave unitarity
[
12
,
31
,
32
]
; numerical polology could replace these with a measure derived from quantum field theory, leaving the likelihood
\mathcal{L}(D|\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
to the established machinery.

Outlook

The approach has several limiting factors. Principally, we do not consider the effects of curvature, or background values of the fields. Whilst this hinders some cosmological applications, it does not preclude them, since background values can often be substituted in phenomenological likelihood pipelines. Superradiance provides a good example of this, since the formulae in
Appendix

D
were derived in Kerr spacetime.

On the other hand, it can be dangerous to transplant effective field theories between regimes in this way. Programmes already exist for systematically constructing models in the early
[
34
,
113
]
and late
[
36
,
54
,
50
]
Universe, where the Hubble flow alters the symmetry and introduces a scale around which the effective theory is organised. The validity of the dark energy likelihood in
Appendix

E
may be limited by these considerations.

As a possible future approach to cosmological backgrounds, note that the spin-projection operator formalism of
[
110
,
85
,
86
,
101
,
100
,
70
,
66
,
67
,
81
,
92
,
77
,
78
,
82
,
83
]
— upon which the present method relies — was recently extended to maximally symmetric spacetimes
[
62
]
. Similarly, the technical details of the algorithm have been worked out only for bosonic fields, so (e.g.) fermionic dark matter is not yet accessible: the extension to fermions is likely to be straightforward, because spin-projection operators admit half-integer representations
[
63
]
.

Lastly, whilst the possibility of numerically computing quantum corrections from interactions has been demonstrated (see
Sections

II.4
and
F
), the assembly of the full interaction likelihood is left to the companion paper.

\mathchoice{\mathcal{T}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{T}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{T}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{T}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\beta}}}}\equiv\mathchoice{\mathcal{T}^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{T}^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{T}^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{T}^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}{\beta}}}}
and
\mathchoice{\mathcal{Q}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{Q}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{Q}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{Q}^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{\beta}}}}\equiv\mathchoice{\mathcal{Q}^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}{\beta}}}}{\mathcal{Q}^{{{\alpha}\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}\mathchoice{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[4.53441pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[2.77156pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.97969pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{\mathchoice{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[5.19876pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.13454pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.23895pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}{\alpha}{\beta}}}}
