. If either of these fields are propagating in our Universe, it is reasonable to expect that their free limits are captured by
Eq.

37
.

Appendix C
Model dimensionality

Participation ratio

The model dimensionality on the
S^{N-1}
hypersphere, i.e.
d-1
, is approximated for each posterior sample
i
as the participation ratio of the principal singular values of the neighbouring samples.

Concretely, for a chosen neighbourhood size
k_{\text{NN}}
we form the
k_{\text{NN}}\times N
matrix
\mathsf{X}(i,k_{\text{NN}})
whose rows are the
k_{\text{NN}}
nearest neighbours of sample
i
(in the
N
-dimensional
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space of the parent action, for which the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
are Cartesian coordinates), and take its singular-value decomposition
\mathsf{X}(i,k_{\text{NN}})-\overline{\mathsf{X}}(i,k_{\text{NN}})\equiv\mathsf{U}(i,k_{\text{NN}})\cdot\mathrm{diag}\!\big(s_{a}(i,k_{\text{NN}})\big)\cdot\mathsf{V}(i,k_{\text{NN}})^{\text{T}}
. The local intrinsic dimension is then defined by

d_{\text{PR}}(i,k_{\text{NN}})\;\equiv\;\frac{\big(\sum_{a}s_{a}(i,k_{\text{NN}})^{2}\big)^{\!2}}{\sum_{a}s_{a}(i,k_{\text{NN}})^{4}}+1.

(38)

The
+1
correction on the RHS of
Eq.

38
ensures that the result corresponds to the dimensionality of the hypersurface in the full
N
-dimensional
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space, rather than the slice seen on the
S^{N-1}
surface that contains the chain. This process is performed for a range of
k_{\text{NN}}
values, with the resulting histograms shown in
Fig.

8
.

Density estimation

Because unitarity is a boolean property, it is important that the prior distribution vanishes in the sick region, whilst being uniform within the healthy region. Uniformity, however, must be defined with respect to some underlying set of coordinates.

For untuned theories, the algorithm in
Appendix

G
samples on the
S^{N-1}
‘sky’, and so it is natural to enforce uniformity with respect to the hyperspherical measure. The reweighting is performed by inverting a
k
NN density estimate. For a chain that occupies a sub-manifold of intrinsic dimension
d
inside the
N
-dimensional
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
-space, the local density at sample
i
is proportional to
k_{\text{NN}}/r(i,k_{\text{NN}})^{d}
, where
r(i,k_{\text{NN}})
is the distance from sample
i
to its
k_{\text{NN}}
nearest neighbour. The importance weight is then the inverse density
r(i,k_{\text{NN}})^{d}
.

The single integer exponent
d
may be approximated by
d_{\text{PR}}(i,k_{\text{NN}})
, as given in
Eq.

38
(specifically, with the choice
k_{\text{NN}}=20
).
Fig.

9
illustrates, for the spin-two (i.e. Fierz–Pauli) branch of
Eq.

12
, that the reweighted chain adheres to the hyperspherical measure as intended. Further details are available at
[
15
]
.

Figure 8:
Effective model dimensionality of the branches in
Eqs.

11
,
12
,
37a
and
37b
. The estimates stabilise with increasing number of nearest neighbours, with noise arising from the curvature of the hypersurfaces in the embedding hyperspheres. The asymptotic values are read off in
Table

1
.

Figure 9:
Uniform ‘sky-coverage’ of the spin-two (Fierz–Pauli) branch of
Eq.

12
, restricted to the analytic unitary portion of the two-dimensional sheet parameterised by the angle
\varphi
of
Eq.

15
and the trace-shift
\sigma
of
Eq.

16
. The coloured contours are obtained as KDEs (orange for the unweighted chain, red for the final, reweighted chain); grey contours indicate the raw density of the hyperspherical measure.

Appendix D
Superradiance pipeline

Theoretical development

Following the framework of Hoof
et al.

[
61
]
, the weight applied to each posterior sample of spin-zero mass
m
is the ‘survival probability’ that the chosen BH’s measured mass and spin is compatible with the existence of an ultralight scalar of that mass. The stellar-mass X-ray binary M33 X-7
[
75
]
is modelled as a Kerr BH; the data comprise 1838 joint posterior samples of the BH mass
M_{\text{BH}}
and (dimensionless) angular momentum
J
, expressed in terms of the spin parameter
a_{*}\equiv 8\pi M_{\text{Pl}}^{2}\,J/M_{\text{BH}}^{2}
.
9
9

9

As a limitation, we inherit these samples from the
BHSR
package of
[
61
]
, which obtained them by digitising a figure in
[
75
]
.

In the absence of interactions, the scalar mode near the BH must have Klein–Gordon dynamics, and should be well described by the collection of quantum states of the form
\left\lvert n,l,m_{l}\right\rangle
, where
n
,
l
and
m_{l}
are the principal, orbital and magnetic quantum numbers, respectively. Superradiant instability corresponds to an exponential growth in the state occupation number
N\approx\exp\left(\Gamma_{\text{SR}}t\right)
, where
t
is the time elapsed and
\Gamma_{\text{SR}}
is the superradiance rate.

For fixed
l
, we assume
\Gamma_{\text{SR}}
to be maximised when

n=l+1,\qquad m_{l}=l.

(39)

Each of
1\leq l\leq 6
is compared with the dimensionless gravitational coupling

\alpha\;\equiv\;\frac{M_{\text{BH}}\,m}{8\pi\,M_{\text{Pl}}^{2}},

(40)

in which
M_{\text{Pl}}\approx$2.43\text{\times}{10}^{18}\text{\,}\mathrm{GeV}$
is the reduced Planck mass. If
\alpha/l>1/2
the bound-state assumptions underlying the analytic approximations to
\Gamma_{\text{SR}}
break down, and we conservatively assume no growth (i.e. skip the state).

Otherwise, we use the approximations of
[
14
]
, i.e.

\displaystyle\Gamma_{\text{SR}}\;\approx

\displaystyle y\,z\,c_{l}\,\omega_{1}\!\prod_{k=1}^{l}\big[k^{2}(1-a_{*}^{2})+y^{2}\big],

(41)

\displaystyle y\;\equiv

\displaystyle l\,a_{*}-2\,r_{+}\,\omega_{0},

\displaystyle z\;\equiv

\displaystyle\big[\alpha^{2}\,(1-\omega_{0}^{2}/m^{2})\big]^{l+1/2},

where
r_{+}\equiv\big(M_{\text{BH}}/(8\pi\,M_{\text{Pl}}^{2})\big)(1+\sqrt{1-a_{*}^{2}})
is the outer-horizon radius of the Kerr spacetime in Boyer–Lindquist coordinates. The leading and subleading bound-state frequencies
\omega_{0}
and
\omega_{1}
in
Eq.

41
are

\displaystyle\omega_{0}\;\equiv\;

\displaystyle m\,\bigg[1-2\alpha^{2}\Big[(l+1)^{2}+4\alpha^{2}

\displaystyle\qquad+(l+1)\sqrt{(l+1)^{2}+8\alpha^{2}}\Big]^{-1}\bigg]^{\!1/2},

(42a)

\displaystyle\omega_{1}\;\equiv\;

\displaystyle\frac{m^{2}-\omega_{0}^{2}}{(l+1)\,\omega_{0}}\,\bigg[1+\frac{4\alpha^{2}(2\omega_{0}^{2}-m^{2})}{m^{2}(l+1)^{2}}\bigg]^{-1},

(42b)

while the combinatorial prefactor is

c_{l}\;\equiv\;\frac{2^{4l+2}\,(l!)^{2}}{(2l+1)!\,(2l)!^{\,2}}.

(43)

Note that the maximum-rate conditions of
Eq.

39
have been substituted into
Eqs.

41
,
42
and
43
, whilst the formulae available in
[
14
]
are more general.

Reweighting

A given state
l
is taken to appreciably modify the BH characteristics over the BH timescale
t_{\text{BH}}
if and only if

\Gamma_{\text{SR}}\,t_{\text{BH}}\;>\;\log N_{\text{fin}},

(44)

where the e-folding budget
\log N_{\text{fin}}
corresponds, somewhat arbitrarily, to the extraction of a dimensionless spin
\Delta a_{*}=0.1
away from the BH and into the growing boson ‘cloud’. This budget was found in
[
11
]
to be

N_{\text{fin}}\;\equiv\;10^{76}\,\Big(\frac{\Delta a_{*}}{0.1}\Big)\,\Big(\frac{M_{\text{BH}}}{10\,M_{\odot}}\Big)^{\!2}\,\frac{1}{l}.

(45)

The estimated age of the M33 X-7 system is taken as
t_{\text{BH}}=$3\text{\,}\mathrm{Myr}$
(see e.g.
[
52
,
61
]
).

A posterior sample is judged incompatible with the boson if
any
state satisfies the growth criterion
Eq.

44
. The weight applied to each sample is then the relative fraction of the surviving posterior samples, which can be interpreted as the survival probability of the BH. Further details are available at
[
15
]
.

Appendix E
Dark energy pipeline

Theoretical development

A homogeneous scalar field of mass
m
in a cosmological background obeys a damped Klein--Gordon equation
10
10

10

Note that the scalar
\phi
appearing in
Eq.

46
represents the final propagating degree of freedom in the particle spectrum: it cannot be immediately identified with the field appearing in
Eq.

9
, since the propagating mode may contain spin-zero contributions from the higher-rank fields in the action.

\ddot{\phi}+3H\dot{\phi}+V^{\prime}(\phi)=0,\qquad V(\phi)\equiv\frac{1}{2}m^{2}\phi^{2},

(46)

where
H
is the Hubble number, so that the discriminant
9H^{2}-4m^{2}
partitions the dynamics into an overdamped (frozen) regime for
m<3H/2
and an underdamped (oscillating) regime for
m>3H/2

[
108
,
76
]
. The scalar field has density and pressure given by

\rho_{\text{de}}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\dot{\phi}^{2}+V(\phi),\qquad P_{\text{de}}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\dot{\phi}^{2}-V(\phi).

(47)

In the overdamped regime we assume slow-roll, i.e.

\dot{\phi}\;\approx\;-\,\frac{V^{\prime}(\phi)}{3H}\;=\;-\,\frac{m^{2}\phi}{3H},

(48)

and substituting
Eq.

48
into
Eq.

47
yields the corresponding equation of state

w_{\text{de}}\;\equiv\;\frac{P_{\text{de}}}{\rho_{\text{de}}}\;=\;\frac{m^{2}-9H^{2}}{m^{2}+9H^{2}},\qquad(m<3H/2).

(49)

Meanwhile, for
m>3H/2
the field undergoes coherent oscillations and a WKB time-average gives the matter-like result
w_{\text{de}}=0

[
108
]
. For this analysis, the two regimes are stitched

w_{\text{de}}(m,H)\equiv\begin{cases}\dfrac{m^{2}-9H^{2}}{m^{2}+9H^{2}},&m<3H/2,\\[6.0pt]
0,&m\geq 3H/2,\end{cases}

(50)

though a more thorough time-averaged integration would avoid the jump at the transition.

The dark energy density obeys the continuity equation
\dot{\rho}_{\text{de}}+3H(1+w_{\text{de}})\rho_{\text{de}}=0
, with formal solution

\displaystyle f_{\text{de}}(z,m)

\displaystyle\equiv\;\frac{\rho_{\text{de}}(z;m)}{\rho_{\text{de}}(0;m)}

(51)

\displaystyle=\;\exp\!\left[\,3\!\int_{0}^{z}\!\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}\,\frac{1+w_{\text{de}}(m,H(z^{\prime}))}{1+z^{\prime}}\,\right],

reducing to
f_{\text{de}}\to 1
in the
\Lambda
CDM limit. Strictly,
H(z^{\prime})
in the integrand depends on
f_{\text{de}}
itself; we evaluate it on a fiducial
\Lambda
CDM background
\Omega_{\text{m}}^{\text{fid}}\equiv 0.315
and
H_{0}^{\text{fid}}\equiv$67.4\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}\text{\,}{\mathrm{Mpc}}^{-1}$
(see
[
5
]
), such that

H_{\text{fid}}(z)\equiv H_{0}^{\text{fid}}\sqrt{\Omega_{\text{m}}^{\text{fid}}(1+z)^{3}+(1-\Omega_{\text{m}}^{\text{fid}})}.

(52)

Plugging
f_{\text{de}}
from
Eq.

51
into the first Friedmann equation at the sampled
\Omega_{\text{m}}
gives the model’s Hubble rate

\displaystyle E

\displaystyle(z;\Omega_{\text{m}},m)\;\equiv\;\frac{H(z)}{H_{0}}

(53)

\displaystyle=\;\sqrt{\Omega_{\text{m}}(1+z)^{3}+(1-\Omega_{\text{m}})\,f_{\text{de}}(z,m)}.

Reweighting

Once the input in
Eq.

53
is computed, the remainder of the pipeline is adapted from Ormondroyd
et al.

[
87
,
88
]
. The three BAO distance ratios reported by DESI in
[
2
]
are

\displaystyle\frac{D_{H}(z)}{r_{\text{d}}}

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{H_{0}r_{\text{d}}\,E(z)},

(54a)

\displaystyle\frac{D_{M}(z)}{r_{\text{d}}}

\displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{H_{0}r_{\text{d}}}\!\!\int_{0}^{z}\!\!\frac{\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}}{E(z^{\prime})},

(54b)

\displaystyle\frac{D_{V}(z)}{r_{\text{d}}}

\displaystyle\equiv\left(z\,\Big(\frac{D_{M}}{r_{\text{d}}}\Big)^{\!2}\frac{D_{H}}{r_{\text{d}}}\right)^{\!1/3},

(54c)

in which
r_{\text{d}}
is the comoving sound horizon at the baryon-drag epoch, and
H_{0}r_{\text{d}}
appears as a multiplicative nuisance parameter. For Pantheon and SH0ES
[
99
]
, the observable is the apparent magnitude

\displaystyle m_{\text{b}}(z_{\text{hd}},z_{\text{hel}})\;\equiv

\displaystyle 5\,\log_{10}\!\!\left[\,(1+z_{\text{hel}})\!\int_{0}^{z_{\text{hd}}}\!\frac{\mathrm{d}z^{\prime}}{E(z^{\prime})}\,\right]

(55)

\displaystyle+\mathcal{M},

where
z_{\text{hd}}
is the redshift corrected for the peculiar motions of the source and observer,
z_{\text{hel}}
is the heliocentric redshift, and
\mathcal{M}
is a constant calibration offset.

The DESI data gives thirteen values for the quantities on the LHS of
Eq.

54
, spanning seven values of
z
, together with a covariance matrix
\mathsf{C}_{\text{BAO}}
. For any values of
m
,
\Omega_{\text{m}}
and
H_{0}r_{\text{d}}
we build the model residual vector
\mathsf{r}
from the RHS of
Eq.

54
and compute the log-likelihood

\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{BAO}}(m,\Omega_{\text{m}},H_{0}r_{\text{d}})\equiv-\frac{1}{2}\ \mathsf{r}^{\text{T}}\cdot\mathsf{C}_{\text{BAO}}^{-1}\cdot\mathsf{r}.

(56)

For the supernovae, we take the cut of 1371 entries on the LHS of
Eq.

55
for which
z_{\text{hd}}>0.023
, so as to exclude observations that might be swept up in the local flow. The predictions are made using only the first term on the RHS of
Eq.

55
, since the offset
\mathcal{M}
is unknown and must be marginalised analytically. The log-likelihood is then

\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{SNe}}(m,\Omega_{\text{m}})\equiv-\frac{1}{2}\ \mathsf{r}^{\text{T}}\cdot\widetilde{\mathsf{C}}_{\text{SNe}}^{-1}\cdot\mathsf{r},

(57)

where the
projected
inverse covariance is defined by

\widetilde{\mathsf{C}}_{\text{SNe}}^{-1}\;\equiv\;\mathsf{C}_{\text{SNe}}^{-1}\;-\;\frac{\mathsf{C}_{\text{SNe}}^{-1}\cdot\mathsf{n}\cdot\mathsf{n}^{\text{T}}\cdot\mathsf{C}_{\text{SNe}}^{-1}}{\mathsf{n}^{\text{T}}\cdot\mathsf{C}_{\text{SNe}}^{-1}\cdot\mathsf{n}},

(58)

and
\mathsf{n}
is the all-ones column vector — the construction in
Eq.

58
is ‘desensitized’ to the global calibration shift, and can be viewed as the sought analytic marginalisation of
\mathcal{M}
.

The remaining nuisance parameters in
Eqs.

56
and
57
are
\Omega_{\text{m}}
and
H_{0}r_{\text{d}}
. These are integrated out on a generous (see again
[
5
]
)
50\times 50
grid covering
\Omega_{\text{m}}\in[0.01,0.99]
and
H_{0}r_{\text{d}}\in[$3650\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$,$18\,250\text{\,}\mathrm{km}\text{\,}{\mathrm{s}}^{-1}$]
, by

\displaystyle\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{mar}}(m)

\displaystyle\;\equiv\;\log\!\!\sum_{i,j}w_{ij}\,\exp\Big[\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{SNe}}\big(m,\Omega_{\text{m}}^{(i)}\big)

\displaystyle+\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{BAO}}\big(m,\Omega_{\text{m}}^{(i)},(H_{0}r_{\text{d}})^{(j)}\big)\Big],

(59)

where
w_{ij}
contains trapezoidal weights and grid spacings.

The dark energy weight is
\exp\!\big[\Delta\log\mathcal{L}(m)\big]
, where

\Delta\log\mathcal{L}(m)\;\equiv\;\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{mar}}(m)-\log\mathcal{L}_{\text{mar}}^{\Lambda\text{CDM}},

(60)

and the
\Lambda
CDM reference is the same marginalisation as in
Eq.

59
, but evaluated with
w_{\text{de}}=-1
identically, i.e.
f_{\text{de}}=1
. Further details are available at
[
15
]
.

Appendix F
Interactions

Derivative interactions

By perturbatively expanding the Einstein–Hilbert term, the cubic and quartic interactions which build on top of the free kinetic sector of
Eq.

(61b)

Algebraic interactions

We can also add to
Eq.

3
the cubic and quartic interactions that are purely algebraic. These require the addition of new couplings beyond those of the general tensor theory in
Eq.

12
, and we write

Appendix G
Untuned implementation

Scope

The main ideas from
Section

III
are combined in a prototype system which takes as input some
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
corresponding to an untuned theory of the kind considered in
Section

II.2
. The output is a sample chain corresponding to theories which (i) propagate exclusively one healthy pole in some user-specified
J^{P}
sector, and (ii) comprehensively explore the coupling space. For simplicity,
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
is assumed not to contain any gauge symmetries.

Platforms

An initial application of computer algebra is required to extract the symbolic
\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}^{{{(n)}}}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta)
from
\mathcal{S}(\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta})
, and this problem was previously solved for any theory of the form given in
Eq.

1
by the
Wolfram Language
implementation in
[
17
,
16
]
. The remainder of the pipeline is implemented in
Python
, specifically within the
JAX
framework, which enables just-in-time compilation of all components.
11
11

11

The use of
JAX
throughout opens the door, in principle, to an eventual GPU acceleration of the algorithm. Note that, for all the models considered in this work, the sampling procedure has a walltime of minutes on a single CPU core at double precision.

Vandermonde inversion

Since
\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)
is Hermitian for real
k
, its determinant is a polynomial in even powers of
k
and so admits the expansion

\det\mathchoice{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}{\mathsf{O}_{{{{J^{P}}}}}}(\theta;k)=\sum_{j=0}^{n_{J^{P}}}\,\mathchoice{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}(\theta)\,z^{j},\qquad z\equiv k^{2}.

(64)

The symbolic computation of
Eq.

64
in the
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
is to be avoided, since it may contain many thousands of monomials. At each sampled
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
, the determinant is thus evaluated numerically at
n_{J^{P}}+1
‘test’ momenta given by

\mathchoice{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}=i,\quad\mathchoice{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{k^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}=\sqrt{\mathchoice{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}},\qquad i=0,1,\ldots,n_{J^{P}}.

(65)

The coefficients
\mathchoice{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}(\theta)
in
Eq.

64
are then recovered by inverting the Vandermonde system

d_{i}\equiv\sum_{j=0}^{n_{J^{P}}}\,\mathchoice{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}(\theta)\,\mathchoice{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}{z^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[2.82928pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[1.68811pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[1.2058pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{i}}}}^{j}\;=\;\sum_{j}\mathchoice{V^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.98645pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.84746pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{ij}}}}{V^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.98645pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.84746pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{ij}}}}{V^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.98645pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.84746pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{ij}}}}{V^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.98645pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.84746pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{ij}}}}\,\mathchoice{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}(\theta),

(66)

where
\mathchoice{V^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.98645pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.84746pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{ij}}}}{V^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.98645pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.84746pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{ij}}}}{V^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.98645pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.84746pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{ij}}}}{V^{{\mathchoice{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\displaystyle$}}{\makebox[6.54285pt][c]{$\textstyle$}}{\makebox[3.98645pt][c]{$\scriptstyle$}}{\makebox[2.84746pt][c]{$\scriptscriptstyle$}}}}_{{{ij}}}}\equiv i^{j}
. This matrix depends only on
n_{J^{P}}
, not on
\mathchoice{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}{\theta}
, so its inverse can be precomputed.

Sampling

To make sure that only the target pole is propagating, it suffices to send all other poles to infinity. The residual vector
\mathsf{r}(\theta)
is constructed by stacking all the
\mathchoice{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{j}}}}(\theta)
which are required to vanish in order to produce this decoupling. This means that the index
j
ranges over all
j\geq 1
for non-target
J^{P}
and over
j\geq 2
for the target sector. Nested sampling is then performed, with the likelihood

\log\mathcal{L}(\text{QFT}|\theta)=-\lvert\mathsf{r}(\theta)\rvert^{2}.

(67)

Note that
Eq.

67
is actually somewhat simpler than our proposal for the tuned case in
Eq.

33
.

We use the
BlackJAX
nested sampler
[
27
,
114
]
with
10^{4}
live points and
5(N-1)
inner steps, deleting
10^{3}
points at each iteration, and with a log-likelihood threshold of
-10^{-10}
. The prior is uniform on the hypersphere, and a geodesic (i.e., great circle) stepper function respects this natural measure.

As mentioned in
Section

III
, nested sampling is not inherently good at root-finding. Rather, it efficiently samples distributions in high-
N
parameter spaces. Here, nested sampling is used to rapidly produce an initial pool of samples whose volume is distributed around small values of
\mathsf{r}(\theta)
. It is expected that a large fraction of this pool will be sufficiently optimised for subsequent refinement, by methods which scale less well with
N
.

Refining

For each of the samples in the resulting chain, the residual vector
\mathsf{r}(\theta)
is further reduced through Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) optimisation. This procedure requires the Jacobian

\mathsf{J}(\theta)\equiv\frac{\partial\mathsf{r}(\theta)}{\partial\theta},

(68)

which can be obtained by forward-mode automatic differentiation through
Eqs.

64
,
65
and
66
.

We use the
Optimistix
LM implementation
[
97
]
, with up to
30
iterations, and relative and absolute tolerances of
10^{-12}
. Samples for which the LM process fails are dropped from the chain, along with samples for which the process yields a final
\lvert\mathsf{r}(\theta)\rvert>10^{-6}
.

Measuring

By construction, the refined samples are known to propagate one (relatively) light pole, with all other poles separated by a substantial mass hierarchy. The masses themselves have not yet been computed, however. This is done directly by the Frobenius companion matrix method, since the
\mathchoice{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{i}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{i}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{i}}}}{c^{{{{J^{P}}}}}_{{{i}}}}(\theta)
themselves are by this point known numerically. The residues are then computed from
Eq.

30
.

In summary, the sampling and refining procedures identify precise points on the target hypersurface, whilst measuring determines the hypersurface boundaries.

Reweighting

The distribution of the surviving points on the hypersurface is affected by
\mathsf{r}(\theta)
and its gradient through
Eqs.

67
and
68
, and this is an unavoidable consequence of sampling and root-finding. Since the points themselves are fundamentally produced at cost in our approach, the ‘cheapest’ procedure is to reweight them in the final chain. A
k
-nearest-neighbour (
k
NN) density estimate is used to restore uniformity with respect to the original prior on the hypersphere; the details are provided in
Appendix

C
. Further details are available at
[
15
]
.
